newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU finance ministers prepare to meet on lira.
newsitem.headline: EU finance ministers prepare to meet on lira.

text.p: European Union finance ministers prepared on Saturday for a crisis meeting in Brussels after talks on bringing the Italian lira back into Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) ran into difficulty.

Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi told the Italian ANSA news agency it was probable that EU finance ministers would have to meet on Sunday. An EU official said the ministers had already been put on stand-by.
"Either it finishes this evening or much more probably there will be a supplement to the talks involving finance ministers," Prodi said.
Monetary sources participating in a meeting of the EU's monetary committee of senior central bank and finance ministry officials in Brussels indicated there was little chance of immediate agreement.
"The positions are still far apart," one source said, referring to disagreement among the EU countries about what rate the lira should have in the currency grid.
Rome hopes a return to the ERM will enhance its chances of qualifying for the single European currency in 1999. A stable two-year stint within the ERM is one of the qualifying criteria.
The ERM is designed to allow member currencies to trade within bands against each other -- for the most part fluctuating by no more than 15 percent from a central rate.
Eleven of the EU's 15 countries are currently members, with only Italy, Sweden, Britain and Greece remaining outside.
Both Italy and Britain were forced out in 1992 after a severe currency crisis nearly brought the system to its knees.

The Italian government does not want the lira to re-enter the grid at too high a level because of the adverse effect on its exports. It has said it would like a rate of between 1,000 and 1,050 lira to the German mark.
Neighbour France, however, wants it in at a less competitive rate because of the impact on its own industry. A figure of 950 lira to the mark has been floated as France's informal goal.
The lira closed around 999 to the mark on Friday.
If the EU fails to agree to let the lira in, the currency is likely to come under intense market pressure on Monday.

German concerns over the future credibility of a single currency have been voiced repeatedly in recent months, punctuated by fears that politics will be the overriding factor in deciding which countries join economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.

European countries which want to include their currencies in the planned Euro from 1999 are rushing to meet targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, budget deficits and public debt in 1997 -- necessary if they are to be at the start.

Most are facing the greatest problems in meeting the fiscal targets, which call for budget deficits to run at a maximum of three percent of gross domestic product and public debt at a maximum of 60 percent of GDP.
Several governments, including Italy, have used controversial one-off budgetary measures to bring their deficits under control.

But some EU monetary officials say that while Italy's turbulent currency history may be a reason to pause, it has nevertheless made enormous strides in the past few years towards becoming a more stable and prosperous economy.
Such an effort cannot be simply brushed aside, they add.
